big: Meena has paid her premium for six years without a claim, and then switches insurer for a cheaper price. She loses something valuable without realising it. Keeping a policy healthy is a long game.

lines: I never made a claim in six years. Did I just waste the money?
No. Cover is what you were buying. And a clean claim record can add to it. But switching carelessly can cost you.

small: ₹10 lakh + 10% of it each year without a claim
alt: Bars showing the sum insured rising by ₹1 lakh each year without a claim
caps: A ₹10 lakh cover with a 10% no-claim bonus.
After one year without a claim, the cover rises to ₹11 lakh at no extra premium.
After three years, it is ₹13 lakh.
Plans differ in the rate and the cap. Check yours.

intro: A few habits protect your cover.
rows: Extra cover or lower premium for years without a claim
Move insurer and keep credit for waiting periods already served
A hospital agreed for cashless claims
Costs before admission and after discharge
note: Apply to port well before renewal, since the move needs time to be approved.

q: Meena has gone six years without a claim. How is the no-claim bonus useful?
opts: It returns all her premiums in cash after six years
It can raise her cover or lower her premium, by plan
It cancels the waiting periods on her policy for good
It lets her claim twice over in the seventh year
why: A bonus raises cover or trims premium. It does not hand back the premiums in cash.
Plans reward years without a claim with extra cover or lower premium, within their own rules.
Waiting periods are separate and are not cancelled by the bonus.
The bonus does not give extra claims. It increases the amount available.

q: Rohan wants to move to another insurer and keep the waiting periods he has already served. What should he use?
opts: Portability, and he should apply well before the renewal date
A fresh purchase, since the old policy ends on the day he leaves
A claim, since every claim carries over to the new insurer
Nothing, since waiting periods always restart on a new policy
why: Portability lets him carry credit for waiting periods served, and it needs time to process.
A fresh purchase restarts the waiting periods, which is the loss he wants to avoid.
Claims do not carry credit. Portability is what preserves the waiting period credit.
Waiting periods restart only when he does not port, so porting avoids that.

q: Meena's policy has pre and post hospitalisation cover of 30 and 60 days. What does it pay for?
opts: Only the days she spends lying in the hospital bed
Her travel costs to the hospital on the day of admission
Medical costs just before admission and after discharge
The premium for the year in which she was in hospital
why: That is the in-patient stay itself. This feature covers the days around it.
Travel is not part of this cover, though some plans add an ambulance.
It pays tests and medicines before admission and follow-up after discharge.
The premium is not refunded just because of a hospital stay at all.

q: A policyholder switches to a cheaper insurer without porting. What is the likely cost?
opts: None, since the new policy is identical to the old one
The old insurer pays all future claims for six months more
The new insurer must cover everything right from day one
Waiting periods may restart, so some illnesses go uncovered
why: Prices may match, but waiting periods do not carry over without porting.
Once the policy ends, the old insurer has no future liability.
A new policy has its own initial and long waiting periods.
A fresh policy restarts waiting periods, so some conditions are excluded again.

pts: A no-claim bonus can raise your cover or lower your premium.
Port your policy instead of buying afresh, so waiting periods carry over.
Check the network hospital list and the pre and post hospitalisation days.
